Abdul Quayum with Md Ismail and JBM Hassan, Advocates -----For the Petitioner.
Momtazuddin Ahmed, Advocate -----For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdul Kader ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Abdullah and others ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued, at the instance of the defendants against the judgment and decree dated 17-7-94 passed in Other Appeal 136 of 1990 by the Additional District Judge, Cox's Bazar, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 20-10-90 passed in Other Suit 50 of 1986 by the Subordinate Judge, Cox's Bazar, dismissing the suit.

2. Opposite parties 1-9 instituted the suit for declaration that the order pussed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner Chittagong on 4-4-84 in Settlement Appeal Case 154 of 1981-82 cancelling the settlement of the suit land made earlier in favour of the plaintiff and the order dated 9-10-85 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Chittagong in S R Case No. 73 of 1984 affirming the judgment and order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff and for further declaration that the judgments and orders dated 23-6-81 passed in Settlement Appeal Nos. 228, 229 and 243 of 1979- 80 and in Settlement Revision case No. 168 of 1981 on 14-11-1982 by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and Divisional Commissioner were legal and plaintiff also prayed for declaration of their title in the suit land.

3. The fact of the case, in short, is that admittedly, the disputed land is the khas land of the Government. The plaintiffs' assertion is that they took the settlement of the suit land in Settlement cases 111-119 of 1978-79 from the Government.

4. Defendants 1-5 filed the Settlement Appeal, against the settlement made to the plaintiff of the suit land. Defendants' appeals are 228, 229, 243 of 1979-80 for cancellation of the settlement of the plaintiff. The appeals were contested. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Chittagong on 23-6-81 dismissed the said appeals of the defendants. Defendant thereafter filed Settlement Revision case No. 168 of 1981 before the Divisional Commissioner against the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and the same was also contested by the present plaintiff. The Divisional Commissioner dismissed the revision by his impugned order dated 14-11-1982. Against that no appeal was taken. The same defendants filed the Settlement case No. 154 of 1981-82 again for cancelling the said settlement of the suit land made to the plaintiffs on the allegation that at the time of their previous objection the settlement to the plaintiff was not complete and, as such, the objection cases they had filed earlier were premature. As to the illegality of the settlement of the plaintiffs, the defendants took similar grounds as were taken earlier.

5. The case was contested by the present plaintiffs. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Chittagong by order dated 4-4-84 cancelled the settlement of the suit land made to the plaintiff. Against that order the plaintiff preferred Settlement Appeal No.73 of 1984 before the Additional Divisional Commissioner. On contest, the appeal was dismissed by order dated 9-10-85 and the order of the Additional Commissioner (Revenue) dated 4-4-84 was affirmed. Thereafter, as it is alleged by the plaintiff, that the defendant 16, Government tried to settle the suit land to different persons in collusion with the defendants 1-15, although it is admitted that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed Other Class Suit 50 of 1986 for declaration, as stated above.

6. Trial Court dismissed the suit. But on appeal the judgment and decree of the trial Court was set aside. The defendants then have come up with the present revision and obtained the Rule.

7. The contention of the defendants as averred in the written statement is that, the suit land was not 'Abadi' land i.e. is not fit for cultivation, consequently the same was not fit for settlement, in the suit land no paddy is grown as claimed by the plaintiff and the defendants were given lease of the suit land on year to year basis, since 1977-78 they were in possession and the claim of possession of the plaintiffs is false.

8. In this context, both parties adduced their evidence both oral and documentary.

9. Trial Court disbelieved the contention of the plaintiff as to their possession and as to the validity of the settlement as alleged to have been given to them.

10. Defendant also took the plea that the plaintiffs are not real tenants and cultivators to give settlement of the suit land to them according to the Government policy. Trial Court found that the settlement was not complete since no deed has been executed by the Government in favour of the plaintiff as yet, It was a mere proposal by the Government even at that stage. Trial Court also held that the order dated 4-4-84 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and the order dated 9-10-89 passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner were valid and not liable to be declared as illegal. Trial Court also held that because the settlement was not mature and it was rather premature, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) and the Divisional Commissioner have rightly cancelled the same. Trial Court also did not believe the possession of the plaintiff.

11. Appellate Court passed a more detailed judgment discussing the case of the parties vividly and precisely. Appellate Court held that the settlement was legal and genuine. Appellate Court also held that only because the lease deed has not been executed by the Government, it cannot be said that the lease was not complete because plaintiffs, according to the appellate Court, were in possession and other formalities including the approval of the lease was completed by legal and proper authority. Appellate Court also found that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) and the Divisional Commissioner illegally cancelled the lease of the plaintiff by the aforesaid impugned orders.

12. The suit land is, no doubt, char land and agricultural in nature which invokes sections 76 and 81 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act being the relevant law for the purpose of settlement of the suit land by way of lease. Section 81(b) has been incorporated in 1971 by amending State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

Section 76(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as under:

"76(1) Settlement and use of land vested in the Government; Except as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, any land which vests in the Government under any of the provisions of this Act shall be absolutely at the disposal of the Government, and the Government shall be competent to make settlement of such land in accordance with such rules as it may make in this behalf or to use or otherwise deal with such land in such manner as it thinks fit;"

Section 81 (b) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is as follows:

"Registration of lease deed. Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 81 and 81A or any other law for the time being in force, no agricultural or non-agricultural tenancy shall in law be created or deemed to have been created, even after acceptance of salami and/or rent from the lessee, till a deed of lease has been executed in favour of the lessee by an authority competent to grant lease of Government khas land or any other Gazetted Officer duly authorized in this behalf and the said lease has been duly registered under the provision of clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908."

It is admitted that the lease deed has not been executed by the Government in favour of the plaintiff. The Sub-Divisional Officer, of course, is found to have approved the proposal vide Exhibits 1, 1C, 5(1), 5(b) in case Nos. 117, 118 and 119 of 1978-79 and so also in the settlement case vide Exhibit.4, and was accepted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner by his order dated 4-4-84, by which the plaintiffs also were directed to give back the possession of the suit land to the Government which proves that the plaintiffs were in possession. The defendant's Eksona (year-by-year basis) could not be proved by any legal document or by any competent witness. Defendants’ possession also could not be established.

13. Possession is not material. It is the question of legal settlement of the suit land. Whether the suit land has been legally settled to the plaintiff or not and whether in the admitted circumstances as mentioned above the plaintiff can claim title in the suit land, are to be decided in this litigation.

14. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff petitioner, submits, that after addition of section 8l(b) of the said Act, law has been changed materially and, according to him, in the present case, the proposal or approval, as the case may be, made by the Sub-Divisional Officer, is not sufficient to complete the lease or settlement of the suit land to the plaintiff. According to him, unless and until the provisions of section 81(b) is complied with through registration of the lease deed the lease, as claimed by the plaintiff, cannot be called a legal and valid one and the approval even if it is given and even plaintiff is in possession, is not sufficient to make the lease complete and legal.

15. On the other hand, Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the defendants opposite parties, submits that the lease was completed. Only for shortage of execution of the lease deed which is a mereformality as the plaintiff was given possession and the plaintiff made liable for payment of compensation by Exhibit.2 series it cannot be said that the lease was not valid one. Mr. Momtazuddin, further submits that only because of pendency of the present litigation necessary deed could not executed and registered. According to him, compliance of section 81(b) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is there. Mr. Momtazuddin also submits that, a declaration of title as prayed for by the plaintiff is not a bar because of section 76(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

16. In this backdrop, I am to decide the litigation involving the question of settlement of the Government khas land.

17. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the opposite parties, referred to (Government Order) GO No.2L-77170/223 RL dated the 2nd April, 1972. He reads Clause S of that GO and this is as follows:

"All previous proposals for settlement of agricultural khas lands at whatever stages they may be, except where the lease deed has already been executed and registered, should be cancelled and the lands covered by such proposals should be leased out in accordance with the provisions of this Government order. In this connection section 81B of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, may be referred to."

The learned Counsel also reads clause 14 of the memorandum as to implementing the Government decision in case of settlement to be made on the basis of said GO.

18. My considered opinion is that the GO or the said clause have not taken away in any manner the force and the meaning of section 81 (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Neither in the said GO nor in the implementation clause anything is there which can supersede the precise and clear prohibition of section 81(b) of the said Act which must be complied, while leasing out agricultural khas land, as in the present case.

19. Here, in this case, whatever may be approval or proposal the settlement of the suit land was not complete as the lease deed as required under section 81 (b) has not been effected. Section 76(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as under:

"No civil Court shall entertain any application or suit concerning any matter relating to the settlement, by any officer of the Government, of any land under sub-section (1)".

So, Government is that highest authority to pass any order as to the settlement Civil Court only can consider, whether the order of the Government is malafide one or suffers from coram non-judice. In that case only the civil Court can interfere by way of declaration, as has been prayed for in the present suit.

<u>20. Mr. Momtazuddin, the learned Counsel; cites a decision in the case of Abdul Majid and others vs Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 23 DLR 203. But that case was decided before the enactment of section 81(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that case judgment was passed on 1st May, 1970. So that one is not applicable in the case Quayum, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, cites the decision in the case of Benzir Ahmed vs Debendra Chandra Saha and others, reported in 4 BLT J 50, wherein the Appellate Division held in para 3 that in a suit for declaration of title mere possession of the property is not sufficient unless the plaintiff can produce a document of title showing his acquisition of right, title and interest in the suit property.</u>

21. In the present suit, the plaintiffs admittedly have not got the deed of lease, their title therefore, is also wanting. In the suit of this nature for declaration of title no relief can be given. It is also held that the Government' authority, namely, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) and Additional Divisional Commissioner were quite competent authority to cancel the lease of the plaintiff in the suit land and there is nothing malafide and their orders do not suffer from coram non-judice.

22. The appellate Court has not considered this vital and legal aspect of the case invoking sections 81(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Appellate Court also failed to appreciate that in this case the alleged settlement was made after 1971 and not before that Appellate Court also failed to appreciate the evidence on record that the settlement to the plaintiff was in the .nature of a proposal and its approval has not been concluded. So, the revenue authority was quite competent to cancel the same being the highest and appropriate authority. The order directing the plaintiff to give back the possession of the suit land to the Government is legal and it is maintained. The plaintiff must give back possession of the suit land to the Government, if not by this time. The suit property can be settled to the genuine persons and claimants afresh in accordance with law.

23. For the reasons and discussion above the Rule has merits and is liable to be made absolute. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court is set aside. The suit is dismissed.

No costs.

End.
